title: House Robber III
question: Why are two DP values needed for each tree node?
answer: Taking a node forbids taking either child, while skipping it allows each child to be taken or skipped. The pair stores the best total for both parent-choice cases.

title: House Robber III
question: How does the tree DP combine child results?
answer: The take-root total is the node value plus both child skip totals. The skip-root total is the sum of the better take/skip value from each child.

title: Counting Bits
question: Why does dp[i] equal dp[i >> 1] plus (i & 1)?
answer: Shifting right removes the least significant bit. The remaining bits contribute dp[i >> 1], and i & 1 adds one exactly when the removed bit was set.

title: Counting Bits
question: Why can the DP be computed in increasing integer order?
answer: The state for i depends on i/2, which is smaller than i and has already been computed. This makes each state constant work.

title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
question: Why should a nested list be expanded in reverse order when using a stack?
answer: A stack is last-in, first-out. Pushing children from right to left leaves the leftmost child on top, preserving the original traversal order.

title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
question: What is the purpose of hasNext() expanding lists before next() returns?
answer: Expansion continues until the next stack item is an integer. That lets next() return the next value without returning nested-list containers.

title: Power of Four
question: How do the two bit tests distinguish powers of four from other integers?
answer: n&(n-1) must be zero so n has exactly one set bit. The mask 0x55555555 permits set bits only at even bit positions, which are the powers-of-four positions.

title: Power of Four
question: Why is checking only for a power of two insufficient?
answer: Every power of four is a power of two, but values such as 2 and 8 are not powers of four. The bit-position mask distinguishes them.

title: Integer Break
question: Why are factors of three used by the greedy integer-break algorithm?
answer: For sufficiently large sums, splitting a factor into threes maximizes the product. A remainder of one is avoided because 3+1 gives a smaller product than 2+2.

title: Integer Break
question: Why are n=2 and n=3 handled separately?
answer: The problem requires at least two positive parts. For these small totals, the best products are 1 and 2, rather than the unsplit value.

title: Reverse String
question: How does the two-pointer method reverse a character array in place?
answer: It swaps the leftmost and rightmost unprocessed characters and moves both pointers inward. Each symmetric pair is exchanged once, requiring constant extra space.

title: Reverse String
question: Why does the loop stop when left is no longer less than right?
answer: At that point every symmetric pair has been swapped. For an odd-length array, the middle character does not need to move.

title: Reverse Vowels of a String
question: How does the algorithm preserve consonant positions?
answer: Each pointer skips non-vowels and only swaps when both point to vowels. Characters skipped by either pointer are never moved.

title: Reverse Vowels of a String
question: Why must the vowel test include uppercase letters?
answer: The input can contain both lowercase and uppercase vowels. Treating both cases as vowels ensures their positions are reversed while consonants remain fixed.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
question: How do frequency buckets help find the k most frequent values?
answer: Each value is placed in a bucket indexed by its frequency. Scanning buckets from the largest frequency down returns high-frequency values without sorting all distinct values.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
question: Why are there at most nums.length + 1 frequency buckets?
answer: No value can appear more times than the total number of array elements, so every frequency lies between one and nums.length.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays
question: Why use sets for the intersection problem?
answer: Sets remove duplicates and provide expected constant-time membership checks. Adding matches to a result set ensures each shared value appears once.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays
question: Is the order of returned intersection values guaranteed?
answer: No. The result is defined by membership and uniqueness, not ordering; iterating a hash set can produce any order.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays II
question: How does frequency counting preserve duplicates correctly?
answer: The map stores the number of unused occurrences from one array. Each match emits one value and decrements its count, limiting output multiplicity to the minimum count in both arrays.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays II
question: Why is a set alone insufficient for Intersection of Two Arrays II?
answer: A set records only whether a value exists and discards multiplicity. A frequency map is needed to output repeated values the correct number of times.
